teaser: One slipped shoulder strap ended a brilliant Paris career in a single afternoon.
review_notes:
Sale to the Met in 1916 for 1,000 pounds, and Sargent's line 'I suppose it is the best thing I have done': check wording.
Quote 'unpaintable beauty and hopeless laziness' from a Sargent letter: check wording.
Lavender powder and rouged ears are reported by contemporaries, not documented by the sitter.
Dimensions used: about 2.1 x 1.1 m (Met: 208.6 x 109.9 cm).
Story that her mother asked Sargent to withdraw the picture: from Ralph Curtis's letter, check.

lesson.text: This canvas was built for one room: the Paris Salon of 1884, a huge glass-roofed hall on the Champs-Élysées where thousands of pictures hung frame to frame, sometimes four rows high. To be noticed there, a painting had to carry across a crowd. Sargent, 28 and ambitious, designed his to work like a poster.

So he made it tall, about 2.1 meters (nearly 7 feet), and stripped it down. A brown wall, a small table, a black dress, and a great expanse of pale skin. From thirty steps away, in a hall crammed with color, that white shape against the dark would stop you.

The woman is Virginie Amélie Gautreau, born in New Orleans and married to a French banker. Paris knew her as a “professional beauty,” someone famous simply for how she looked. She did not order this portrait. Sargent asked her, hoping her fame would rub off on him.

The sittings, at her country house in Brittany in the summer of 1883, went badly. She was bored and kept moving. Sargent complained in a letter about “the unpaintable beauty and hopeless laziness of Madame Gautreau.”
He drew her on a sofa, at the piano, raising a glass. Then he settled on a pose that looks effortless and is in fact a strain to hold. Follow it from the top down.

lesson.title: A difficult pose
lesson.text: Her body faces you, her head turns fully away. Tap to follow the twist.

spots.title: The profile
spots.text: A clean outline, like a face on a coin. She gives the crowd her most famous feature and refuses to look at anyone.

spots.title: The twisted arm
spots.text: Her right arm is turned so the inside of the elbow faces out, fingers pressed on the table. Try it: the shoulder tightens at once.

spots.title: The other hand
spots.text: It gathers the skirt and holds a closed black fan. A thin gold wedding ring catches the light on one finger.

lesson.text: That tension is the point. She is not relaxing for us, she is holding a line, the way a dancer holds a position. Sargent turned a society lady into a silhouette, and the silhouette says: I know you are staring.

Then there is the skin. Gautreau was said to dust herself with lavender-tinted powder, and Sargent painted exactly that: a cool, bluish white, nothing like healthy pink. Only one small part of her kept its natural color.
One spot of warm, natural pink gives away the makeup everywhere else. Can you tap it?

spots.title: The ear
spots.text: Her ear glows reddish pink next to the powdered cheek and neck. Visitors noticed, and joked that the famous beauty was painted twice: once by herself, once by Sargent.

lesson.text: The Salon opened and the plan collapsed. People crowded in front of the picture to laugh and sneer. The dead-white skin looked unhealthy to them, the dress indecent. And one detail, which you cannot see anymore, pushed it over the edge.

In the version shown in 1884, the jeweled strap on her right shoulder had slipped down onto her arm. To Parisians it suggested a woman half undressed. Her mother begged Sargent to take the painting down. He refused, but afterward he repainted the strap where it sits today.
The catalog listed the picture only as “Portrait of Madame ***” to protect her name. It fooled nobody. Everyone in the hall knew who she was, which made the mockery personal.
The scandal was not about nudity, which filled the Salon every year in mythological scenes. It was about a real, recognizable woman shown as proud of her own body.

Commissions in Paris dried up. Within two years Sargent had moved to London for good, where he slowly rebuilt his career and became the most sought-after portraitist of his time. The painting went with him and stayed in his studio for more than thirty years.

spots.title: Diamond crescent
spots.text: A tiny crescent moon sits in her hair, the emblem of Diana, the Roman goddess of the hunt. A fitting badge for a woman who is admired and keeps her distance.

spots.title: The repainted strap
spots.text: This is the strap that once hung off the shoulder. Sargent painted it back in place after the Salon. The chain on the other side was always where you see it.

spots.title: Heart-shaped neckline
spots.text: Black velvet cut low against powdered skin. The contrast between the two is the whole color scheme of the picture.

spots.title: The table
spots.text: A small round table with slim gilded legs. It gives her something to lean on and its curve echoes her shoulders.

spots.title: Black on black
spots.text: The dress is not flat. Velvet above absorbs the light, satin below reflects it in gray streaks. Sargent builds a whole figure from two blacks.

spots.title: Signature
spots.text: Signed and dated 1884 in the corner, in the year he expected this picture to make his name in Paris.

lesson.text: In 1916, shortly after Gautreau died, Sargent sold the portrait to the Metropolitan Museum for 1,000 pounds. He asked that her name stay off it, which is how it became “Madame X.” He told the director: “I suppose it is the best thing I have done.”
So the picture made to conquer one room in Paris ended up owning another one in New York, where people still slow down in front of it. The crowd is back. This time nobody is laughing.

quiz.question: Where was this portrait first shown?
quiz.explanation: Sargent designed it to stand out at the Paris Salon of 1884.

quiz.question: Who asked for the portrait to be painted?
quiz.explanation: It was not a commission: Sargent asked Gautreau to pose.

quiz.question: What did Sargent change after the scandal?
options: He covered her shoulders with a shawl
He repainted a fallen strap back onto the shoulder
quiz.explanation: The strap originally hung down on her arm.

quiz.question: Which detail keeps its natural pink color?
quiz.explanation: The reddish ear contrasts with the lavender-powdered skin.

quiz.question: What does the crescent in her hair refer to?
quiz.explanation: The crescent moon is Diana's emblem.

facts.text: Madame Gautreau paid Sargent a high fee for the portrait.
facts.explanation: She never commissioned it. Sargent asked her to sit.

facts.text: Sargent kept the painting in his own studio for more than thirty years.
facts.explanation: He only sold it to the Metropolitan Museum in 1916.

facts.text: The title “Madame X” was chosen by the Salon jury in 1884.
facts.explanation: The name came in 1916, when Sargent asked the Met to leave her name off.
